## Music And Apparel
Tenement is a three-piece rock band from Appleton. They are often associated with the American hardcore punk scene. Tenement has glided through a mirage of descriptions, everything from noise pop to fuzz punk due to their more experimental, improvisational, high-energy performances.
The great expanse of Wisconsin to this day remains a wild frontier to many. Even to its own sons and daughters, the thought often persists that perhaps there are demons in the woods, or something unknown in the water. It can be no mistake then that Tenement were raised in these woods and drank of this water. Over the course of their nine year career to date, their work ethic and musical ideas have often been attributed to an outsider mentality and a stubborn individualism. The energy they conjure at will might also at times seem just short of some kind of sorcery. Now, with the release of their new double record, Predatory Headlights, their place in the modern world of music has become distinct. They’re no longer only an obscure punk band from the farthest reaches of society’s consciousness, but also one of America’s great outsider pop groups.

## Music And Apparel
The principal songwriter of this trio is Amos Pitsch. He founded the group in 2007 with bassist Jesse Ponkamo, and the two embraced Eric Mayer as their full time drummer some years later. As a live act, they’re an assault on the ears, a confusing spectacle, and a dispensary of remedies for the lonely and misunderstood all at once. In a studio setting, as you’ll hear in Predatory Headlights, their touch is delicate and thoughtful even at its loudest moments. You can hear the strong influence of bands like The Descendents, The Ramones, and even more primitive groups in the playing and execution. But the influence of luminaries such as Ruth Crawford Seeger, William S Fischer, and Robert Kirby are evident in the addition of strings to the pop songs that could stand sturdy on their own even without them. Still upon repeated listening, you might be able to catch an array of other influences, ranging from northern soul to exotica to the avant garde. These are stirred in with ease; something Tenement does naturally as their intention is always steadfast and absolute. In other words, when something needs to be pretty, they make it pretty. And when something needs to be ugly, they leave no gloss, shimmer, or sheen. They strangle the song bird of its TWEET TWEET – and let it cough.

## Music And Apparel
Predatory Headlights was completed over the course of three years with the assistance of engineer and co-producer, Justin Perkins. Pitsch has often cited Perkins’ involvement in early 2000’s groups Yesterday’s Kids and The Obsoletes as a heavy influence. Perkins also worked with Tenement on their 2011 offering, Napalm Dream, as well as acclaimed records by the likes of The Goodnight Loving, The Sugar Stems, and The Mystery Girls. The bulk of Predatory Headlights was written and recorded at BFG in Appleton, Wisconsin – Tenement’s home and personal studio. The house was symbolically demolished within days of finishing the record, and in a fitting display of finality, three years of sweat and nightmares and beauty and dissonance returned to the soil and found its way back into the water and woods with only this document to prove it ever even existed at all. Thanks to Don Giovanni Records, you hold the very document in your hands – Tenement’s newest window into the nature of the human being and the complexity of life: Predatory Headlights.

Tenement and their relation to contemporary punk, hardcore, and DIY was the subject of _The New York Times_ ' June 2015 Popcast; which was hosted by author Ben Ratliff and featured special guests Maria Sherman and Liz Pelly. In reference to Tenement and the DIY scene in which they operate out of, Pelly noted, "It's pretty clear that for these musicians punk is more something they relate to on an ideological level."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenement_(band)#cite_note-12)
In 2016, Tenement was invited to play _Eaux Claires_, an outdoor music festival curated by Justin Vernon of Bon Iver and Aaron Dessner of The National. Pitsch and Tenement really exhibit the independent qualities that Eaux Claires holds so dearly. And while Erykah is an extremely important part of the landscape of this year, everything plays into that. For me it's just interesting to watch those worlds interact and also coexist simultaneously." [[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenement_(band)#cite_note-15)

Actor and comedian Chris Gethard curated a playlist for Brooklyn, New York club Shea Stadium in 2016, compiling his favorite performances at the venue. He included Tenement's 2013 performance of "Spit In The Wind" with the note, "Simply put, they don't make 'em better than Tenement. My wife is significantly cooler than I am and was the one who made it clear to me that Tenement would be one of my favorite bands, and she was totally correct."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenement_(band)#cite_note-16)

## Style and reputation
[edit]
For most of their formative years, members of Tenement lived in and operated the BFG punk house in Appleton, Wisconsin- which hosted hundreds of bands over the course of eight years and served as a recording space for portions of each of their studio albums from 2011 to 2015. Their connection to the house and the relationships they developed with national touring artists that played there cemented their reputation as disciples of DIY culture.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenement_(band)#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenement_(band)#cite_note-18) Despite national acclaim, the house (and the band) remained an underground fixture within the confines of the city of Appleton. I’d always thought that it was meant to be bulldozed and not to be handed over to new tenants. The energy that place held after we’d been there for eight years wasn’t meant to linger in a normal family environment."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenement_(band)#cite_note-20) For many, setting foot in The BFG was an experience that brought them to a closer understanding of what drove Tenement as a group and how they fit- personally and creatively- into the greater scheme of music and art in America. Some saw them as off-the-grid, insular, outlying personas, and others saw them as music savants, students of their record collections, and eccentrics with nearly singular-interest personalities. _RVA Mag_ visited the house in 2010 and wrote: "[Amos'] room, located on the top floor of the BFG House, Appleton’s main house show venue, is indicative of his lifestyle. # Tenement Members, Gear & Sound
## About
**Tenement** is an indie punk and power pop band originating from Appleton, Wisconsin. Formed in 2006, the group is known for its catchy yet intelligent approach to punk music, blending sharp melodies with a willingness to experiment. The band is led by **Amos Pitsch (vocals, guitar)**, who is also notable for his striking collage artwork that adorns the band's releases. Pitsch is joined by **Jesse Ponkamo (bass)**, whom he met in high school, and **Eric Mayer (drums)**, who became a permanent member after initially joining as a temporary replacement. Tenement's discography includes albums like _Napalm Dream_ and _Predatory Headlights_, showcasing their dynamic range and lyrical depth.

# Tenement Members, Gear & Sound
## How to Sound Like Tenement
Tenement’s sound is characterized by its gritty and energetic punk aesthetic, balanced with melodic power pop sensibilities. Their sonic palette is aggressive yet accessible, marked by **crunchy guitar riffs** that often utilize overdrive pedals for a raw, biting tone. The **bass lines are punchy and driving**, providing a solid backbone that complements the frenetic guitar work. Drumming in Tenement’s music is both forceful and dynamic, adding to their high-energy performances. To capture their sound, musicians might focus on utilizing **simple but effective effects** like overdrive and distortion, paired with **high-gain tube amplifiers** to achieve that classic punk intensity. The band's recordings also exhibit a DIY ethos, with production that maintains a live, raw feel — an approach that aspiring musicians can emulate with straightforward recording techniques and minimal post-processing.

As of the 2020 census, the population was 190,705.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-2020-census-55087-2) Its county seat is Appleton.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR6-3)

"Outagamie", a French transliteration of the Anishinaabe term for the Meskwaki (Fox) people, means "dwellers of the other shore" or "dwellers on the other side of the stream",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4) referring to their historic habitation along the St. Lawrence River and south of the Great Lakes. ## Fox Cities at the Center.
Outagamie County sits at the heart of the Fox Cities region, anchored by Appleton and extending through a mix of smaller cities, villages, and townships that together define one of the more economically active corridors in Wisconsin. The Fox River runs through the county from south to north, and the industrial and commercial history built along that waterway has left a legacy of stable employment, established neighborhoods, and a regional identity tied to manufacturing, paper, and professional services.
Appleton anchors the county as its largest city and economic hub, but Outagamie County's strength comes from the range of communities surrounding it. Kaukauna, Kimberly, Freedom, Seymour, and Wrightstown each bring their own school districts, character, and price points to the market, giving buyers genuine options across a spectrum from urban walkability to rural acreage. The Fox Cities metro area, which spans Outagamie, Calumet, and Winnebago counties, consistently ranks among the stronger small metro economies in the Midwest.
Housing in Outagamie County covers significant ground. Buyers in Appleton find an urban market with strong demand and limited inventory. Buyers in the county's smaller communities find more space, independent school districts, and price points that reflect the township rather than the city. The county's location between Green Bay to the north and the broader Milwaukee corridor to the south keeps it connected to two major labor markets while maintaining its own economic weight.

texts.1:
Outagamie County is part of the Appleton Metropolitan Statistical Area, which is itself part of the Appleton-Neenah-OshkoshCombined Statistical Area. It was named for the historic Meskwaki (Fox) people.
"Outagamie", a French transliteration of the Anishinaabe term for the Meskwaki (Fox) people, means "dwellers of the other shore" or "dwellers on the other side of the stream",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4) referring to their historic habitation along the St. Lawrence River and south of the Great Lakes. They occupied considerable territory in Wisconsin before colonization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-5) Outagamie County was created in 1851 and organized in 1852.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6) Before that, it was under the jurisdiction of Brown County.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has an area of 645 square miles (1,670 km 2), of which 638 square miles (1,650 km 2) is land and 7.1 square miles (18 km 2) (1.1%) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR1-7)

*   Shioc River - This river runs merges with the Wolf River in the village of Shiocton.

*   Black Otter Lake - Located in Hortonville, it receives much recreational use by anglers as the county's only lake.
Outagamie County's government consists of an elected County Board of Supervisors, a County Executive, and 36 county agencies and departments.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-outagamie.org-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-9)
The county executive serves as its chief executive officer, participating in the legislative process with the County Board of Supervisors and exercising administrative authority and control over the county's operations, departments, offices, boards, programs, and communications.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-10)
Department heads are appointed by the county executive, subject to the approval of the board of supervisors. The county executive also appoints members to the county's boards and commissions. The county executive sets the annual budget in consultation with and subject to the approval of the board of supervisors.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-11)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-outagamie.org-8)

# Outagamie County
## Fox Cities at the Center.
Outagamie County sits at the heart of the Fox Cities region, anchored by Appleton and extending through a mix of smaller cities, villages, and townships that together define one of the more economically active corridors in Wisconsin. The Fox River runs through the county from south to north, and the industrial and commercial history built along that waterway has left a legacy of stable employment, established neighborhoods, and a regional identity tied to manufacturing, paper, and professional services.
Appleton anchors the county as its largest city and economic hub, but Outagamie County's strength comes from the range of communities surrounding it. Kaukauna, Kimberly, Freedom, Seymour, and Wrightstown each bring their own school districts, character, and price points to the market, giving buyers genuine options across a spectrum from urban walkability to rural acreage. The Fox Cities metro area, which spans Outagamie, Calumet, and Winnebago counties, consistently ranks among the stronger small metro economies in the Midwest.
Housing in Outagamie County covers significant ground. Buyers in Appleton find an urban market with strong demand and limited inventory. Buyers in the county's smaller communities find more space, independent school districts, and price points that reflect the township rather than the city. The county's location between Green Bay to the north and the broader Milwaukee corridor to the south keeps it connected to two major labor markets while maintaining its own economic weight.

Green Bay, center, is the seat of Brown County. The city of Oconto (half cut off at the bottom right) is the county seat of Oconto County. Slightly above and much further right of Oconto is Oconto Falls, also in Oconto County. ### Political representation
[edit]
The current Wisconsin Legislative districts were defined in the law 2023 Wisconsin Act 94, passed by the legislature and signed by the Governor in February 2024. The current congressional districts were defined by the Wisconsin Supreme Court decision _Johnson v. Wisconsin Elections Commission_ in April 2022.
For representation in the U.S. House of Representatives, Brown County falls entirely within [Wisconsin's 8th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_8th_congressional_district "Wisconsin's 8th congressional district"), currently represented by Republican Tony Wied, since November 2024.
In the Wisconsin Senate, Brown County fully contains one Senate district (the 30th), and makes up a portion of two other districts (the 1st and 2nd).
*   the [1st Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 1st Senate district") contains the rural eastern and southern parts of Brown County along with the neighboring Door Peninsula, and is represented by Republican André Jacque of De Pere.  
*   the [2nd Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Senate district") contains the rural northwestern quadrant of Brown County and vast areas of surrounding counties, and is represented by Republican Eric Wimberger of Oconto.  
*   the [30th Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_30th_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 30th Senate district") contains the core urban and suburban areas of Green Bay, De Pere, Ashwaubenon, and Allouez, and is represented by Democrat Jamie Wall of Green Bay.
In the Wisconsin State Assembly, Brown County fully contains three Assembly districts (88th, 89th, and 90th), and makes up a portion of five other districts (the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 6th).

### Racial and ethnic composition
At the 2010 census there were 248,007 people, 98,383 households, and 63,721 families living in the county. The population density was 403 people per square mile (156 people/km 2). There were 104,371 housing units at an average density of 170 units per square mile (66 units/km 2). The racial makeup of the county was 86.5% White, 2.2% Black or African American, 2.7% Native American, 2.7% Asian, 0.0004% Pacific Islander, 3.7% from other races, and 2.2% from two or more races. 7.3% of the population were Hispanic or Latino of any race.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR8-29) Of the 98,383 households 31.0% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 50.0% were married couples living together, 10.2% had a female householder with no husband present, and 35.2% were non-families. 27.7% of households were one person and 8.9% were one person aged 65 or older. The average household size was 2.45 and the average family size was 3.02.
The age distribution was 24.1% under the age of 18, 10.8% from 18 to 24, 26.9% from 25 to 44, 26.6% from 45 to 64, and 11.6% 65 or older. The median age was 36.2 years. For every 100 females, there were 97.80 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 95.70 males.
2000 Census Age Pyramid for Brown County

### Racial and ethnic composition
At the 2000 census there were 226,778 people, 87,295 households, and 57,527 families living in the county. The population density was 429 people per square mile (166 people/km 2). There were 90,199 housing units at an average density of 171 units per square mile (66 units/km 2). The racial makeup of the county was 91.14% White, 1.16% Black or African American, 2.29% Native American, 2.18% Asian, 0.03% Pacific Islander, 1.90% from other races, and 1.30% from two or more races. 3.84% of the population were Hispanic or Latino of any race. 33.8% were of German, 8.9% Polish, 7.8% Belgian and 6.8% Irish ancestry. 93.2% spoke only English at home, 3.8% spoke Spanish and 1.2% Hmong.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR8-29) Of the 87,295 households 33.90% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 53.20% were married couples living together, 8.90% had a female householder with no husband present, and 34.10% were non-families. 26.50% of households were one person and 8.40% were one person aged 65 or older. The average household size was 2.51 and the average family size was 3.08.

### Racial and ethnic composition
The age distribution was 26.10% under the age of 18, 10.50% from 18 to 24, 31.90% from 25 to 44, 20.90% from 45 to 64, and 10.70% 65 or older. The median age was 34 years. For every 100 females, there were 98.90 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 96.90 males.
The legislative branch of Brown County is the 26-member Board of Supervisors. Each member represents a single district and serves a two-year term, with elections held in the spring of even-numbered years. The Board of Supervisors elects a chairman and Vice Chairman from its membership.
The executive branch of Brown County is the County Executive, who is elected in the spring of every other odd-numbered year. The executive appoints department heads with the approval of the County Board. The current county executive is Troy Streckenbach.
Brown County has several other elected officials that are established under the Wisconsin State constitution and are referred to as the "constitutional officers". Constitutional officers are the only partisan elected officials within Brown County government, as the Executive and County Board are non-partisan positions.
The current constitutional officers are:
*   County Executive: Troy Streckenbach (Independent)  
*   Clerk: Sandy Juno (R)  
*   Clerk of Circuit Courts: John Vander Leest (R)  
*   District Attorney: David L. Lasee (R)  
*   Register of Deeds: Cheryl Berken (R)

Brown County and adjacent counties, in the early morning of January 1, 2018, taken from the International Space Station
Green Bay, center, is the seat of Brown County. The city of Oconto (half cut off at the bottom right) is the county seat of Oconto County. Slightly above and much further right of Oconto is Oconto Falls, also in Oconto County. The somewhat larger city above Oconto Falls is Pulaski, which is in Brown County at the very border with Shawano County. Shawano County extends between Pulaski and past the edge of the photograph.
The large city in the top right is Appleton, the county seat of Outagamie County. To the left of Appleton and across the northern edge of Lake Winnebago is Brillion in Calumet County.
The village directly to the left of Green Bay and its immediate suburbs is Denmark, in Brown County. The smaller communities above and slightly to the left of Denmark (including Cooperstown, Maribel, and Kellnersville) are in Manitowoc County.
Luxembourg (larger village in lower left) and Casco (half cut off at lower far left) are in Kewaunee County.
Brown County is rather conservative for an urban county. Since 1968, Brown County has voted for the Republican presidential candidate in all but two elections, 1996 and 2008. Democratic strength is concentrated in the city of Green Bay, while the suburban and rural areas typically vote Republican.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-31)

### Political representation
[edit]
The current Wisconsin Legislative districts were defined in the law 2023 Wisconsin Act 94, passed by the legislature and signed by the Governor in February 2024. The current congressional districts were defined by the Wisconsin Supreme Court decision _Johnson v. Wisconsin Elections Commission_ in April 2022.
For representation in the U.S. House of Representatives, Brown County falls entirely within [Wisconsin's 8th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_8th_congressional_district "Wisconsin's 8th congressional district"), currently represented by Republican Tony Wied, since November 2024.
In the Wisconsin Senate, Brown County fully contains one Senate district (the 30th), and makes up a portion of two other districts (the 1st and 2nd).
*   the [1st Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 1st Senate district") contains the rural eastern and southern parts of Brown County along with the neighboring Door Peninsula, and is represented by Republican André Jacque of De Pere.  
*   the [2nd Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Senate district") contains the rural northwestern quadrant of Brown County and vast areas of surrounding counties, and is represented by Republican Eric Wimberger of Oconto.  
*   the [30th Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_30th_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 30th Senate district") contains the core urban and suburban areas of Green Bay, De Pere, Ashwaubenon, and Allouez, and is represented by Democrat Jamie Wall of Green Bay.
In the Wisconsin State Assembly, Brown County fully contains three Assembly districts (88th, 89th, and 90th), and makes up a portion of five other districts (the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 6th).

### Political representation
*   the [1st Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 1st Assembly district") contains just the northeast corner of Brown County then stretches into Kewaunee and Door counties, and is represented by Republican Joel Kitchens.  
*   the [2nd Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Assembly district") contains the southern half of Brown County and the northern half of neighboring Manitowoc County along with a small portion of Outagamie County, and is represented by Republican Shae Sortwell.  
*   the [4th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_4th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 4th Assembly district") contains the northern Brown County municipalities of Howard and Suamico, and extends north to eastern Oconto County, and is represented by Republican David Steffen.  
*   the [5th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_5th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 5th Assembly district") contains western Brown County and eastern Outagamie County, and is represented by Republican Joy Goeben.  
*   the [6th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_6th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 6th Assembly district") contains the northwestern Brown County municipalities of Pittsfield and Pulaski, then a wide area of the counties to the west, and is represented by Republican Elijah Behnke.  
*   the [88th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_88th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 88th Assembly district") contains all of De Pere, Allouez, and Bellevue, and is represented by Republican Ben Franklin.  
*   the [89th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_89th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 89th Assembly district") contains all of Ashwaubenon and part of the western side of Green Bay, and is represented by Democrat Ryan Spaude.  

### Political representation

The legislative branch of Brown County is the 26-member Board of Supervisors. Each member represents a single district and serves a two-year term, with elections held in the spring of even-numbered years. The Board of Supervisors elects a chairman and Vice Chairman from its membership.
The executive branch of Brown County is the County Executive, who is elected in the spring of every other odd-numbered year. The executive appoints department heads with the approval of the County Board. The current county executive is Troy Streckenbach.
Brown County has several other elected officials that are established under the Wisconsin State constitution and are referred to as the "constitutional officers". Constitutional officers are the only partisan elected officials within Brown County government, as the Executive and County Board are non-partisan positions.
The current constitutional officers are:
*   County Executive: Troy Streckenbach (Independent)  
*   Clerk: Sandy Juno (R)  
*   Clerk of Circuit Courts: John Vander Leest (R)  
*   District Attorney: David L. Lasee (R)  
*   Register of Deeds: Cheryl Berken (R)  
*   Sheriff: Todd Delain (R)  
*   Treasurer: Paul Zeller (R)
In July 2002, the county declared English its official language, voting 17–8 to do so and to increase spending to promote fluency in English.

Green Bay, center, is the seat of Brown County. The city of Oconto (half cut off at the bottom right) is the county seat of Oconto County. Slightly above and much further right of Oconto is Oconto Falls, also in Oconto County. The somewhat larger city above Oconto Falls is Pulaski, which is in Brown County at the very border with Shawano County. Shawano County extends between Pulaski and past the edge of the photograph.
The large city in the top right is Appleton, the county seat of Outagamie County. To the left of Appleton and across the northern edge of Lake Winnebago is Brillion in Calumet County.
The village directly to the left of Green Bay and its immediate suburbs is Denmark, in Brown County. The smaller communities above and slightly to the left of Denmark (including Cooperstown, Maribel, and Kellnersville) are in Manitowoc County.
Luxembourg (larger village in lower left) and Casco (half cut off at lower far left) are in Kewaunee County.
Brown County is rather conservative for an urban county. Since 1968, Brown County has voted for the Republican presidential candidate in all but two elections, 1996 and 2008. Democratic strength is concentrated in the city of Green Bay, while the suburban and rural areas typically vote Republican.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-31)

### Political representation
[edit]
The current Wisconsin Legislative districts were defined in the law 2023 Wisconsin Act 94, passed by the legislature and signed by the Governor in February 2024. The current congressional districts were defined by the Wisconsin Supreme Court decision _Johnson v. Wisconsin Elections Commission_ in April 2022.
For representation in the U.S. House of Representatives, Brown County falls entirely within [Wisconsin's 8th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_8th_congressional_district "Wisconsin's 8th congressional district"), currently represented by Republican Tony Wied, since November 2024.
In the Wisconsin Senate, Brown County fully contains one Senate district (the 30th), and makes up a portion of two other districts (the 1st and 2nd).
*   the [1st Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 1st Senate district") contains the rural eastern and southern parts of Brown County along with the neighboring Door Peninsula, and is represented by Republican André Jacque of De Pere.  
*   the [2nd Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Senate district") contains the rural northwestern quadrant of Brown County and vast areas of surrounding counties, and is represented by Republican Eric Wimberger of Oconto.  
*   the [30th Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_30th_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 30th Senate district") contains the core urban and suburban areas of Green Bay, De Pere, Ashwaubenon, and Allouez, and is represented by Democrat Jamie Wall of Green Bay.
In the Wisconsin State Assembly, Brown County fully contains three Assembly districts (88th, 89th, and 90th), and makes up a portion of five other districts (the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 6th).

### Political representation
*   the [1st Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 1st Assembly district") contains just the northeast corner of Brown County then stretches into Kewaunee and Door counties, and is represented by Republican Joel Kitchens.  
*   the [2nd Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Assembly district") contains the southern half of Brown County and the northern half of neighboring Manitowoc County along with a small portion of Outagamie County, and is represented by Republican Shae Sortwell.  
*   the [4th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_4th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 4th Assembly district") contains the northern Brown County municipalities of Howard and Suamico, and extends north to eastern Oconto County, and is represented by Republican David Steffen.  
*   the [5th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_5th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 5th Assembly district") contains western Brown County and eastern Outagamie County, and is represented by Republican Joy Goeben.  
*   the [6th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_6th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 6th Assembly district") contains the northwestern Brown County municipalities of Pittsfield and Pulaski, then a wide area of the counties to the west, and is represented by Republican Elijah Behnke.  
*   the [88th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_88th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 88th Assembly district") contains all of De Pere, Allouez, and Bellevue, and is represented by Republican Ben Franklin.  
*   the [89th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_89th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 89th Assembly district") contains all of Ashwaubenon and part of the western side of Green Bay, and is represented by Democrat Ryan Spaude.

### Political representation
[edit]
The current Wisconsin Legislative districts were defined in the law 2023 Wisconsin Act 94, passed by the legislature and signed by the Governor in February 2024. The current congressional districts were defined by the Wisconsin Supreme Court decision _Johnson v. Wisconsin Elections Commission_ in April 2022.
For representation in the U.S. House of Representatives, Brown County falls entirely within [Wisconsin's 8th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_8th_congressional_district "Wisconsin's 8th congressional district"), currently represented by Republican Tony Wied, since November 2024.
In the Wisconsin Senate, Brown County fully contains one Senate district (the 30th), and makes up a portion of two other districts (the 1st and 2nd).
*   the [1st Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 1st Senate district") contains the rural eastern and southern parts of Brown County along with the neighboring Door Peninsula, and is represented by Republican André Jacque of De Pere.  
*   the [2nd Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Senate district") contains the rural northwestern quadrant of Brown County and vast areas of surrounding counties, and is represented by Republican Eric Wimberger of Oconto.  
*   the [30th Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_30th_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 30th Senate district") contains the core urban and suburban areas of Green Bay, De Pere, Ashwaubenon, and Allouez, and is represented by Democrat Jamie Wall of Green Bay.
In the Wisconsin State Assembly, Brown County fully contains three Assembly districts (88th, 89th, and 90th), and makes up a portion of five other districts (the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 6th).

### Political representation
*   the [1st Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 1st Assembly district") contains just the northeast corner of Brown County then stretches into Kewaunee and Door counties, and is represented by Republican Joel Kitchens.  
*   the [2nd Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Assembly district") contains the southern half of Brown County and the northern half of neighboring Manitowoc County along with a small portion of Outagamie County, and is represented by Republican Shae Sortwell.  
*   the [4th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_4th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 4th Assembly district") contains the northern Brown County municipalities of Howard and Suamico, and extends north to eastern Oconto County, and is represented by Republican David Steffen.  
*   the [5th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_5th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 5th Assembly district") contains western Brown County and eastern Outagamie County, and is represented by Republican Joy Goeben.  
*   the [6th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_6th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 6th Assembly district") contains the northwestern Brown County municipalities of Pittsfield and Pulaski, then a wide area of the counties to the west, and is represented by Republican Elijah Behnke.  
*   the [88th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_88th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 88th Assembly district") contains all of De Pere, Allouez, and Bellevue, and is represented by Republican Ben Franklin.  
*   the [89th Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_89th_Assembly_district "Wisconsin's 89th Assembly district") contains all of Ashwaubenon and part of the western side of Green Bay, and is represented by Democrat Ryan Spaude.
